name: Question 11
problem:
Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfy the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ satisfy the inhomogeneous system
${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t)+f(t).$
Which of the following is **always** a solution of the same inhomogeneous system?

- ${x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)$
- $5\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$
- $-3\cdot {x}_{2}(t)-{x}_{p}(t)$
worked_solution:
Recall that if ${x}_{h}(t)$ satisfies a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution to an inhomogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ then ${x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$ is also a solution to the same inhomogeneous system.

Additonally, the *linearity principle* for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if ${x}_{1}(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t),…,{x}_{k}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ then any linear combination 

$$
{c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)+⋯+{c}_{k}{x}_{k}(t)
$$

with ${c}_{1},{c}_{2},…,{c}_{k}\in R$ is also a solution of the same homogeneous system. 

With that in mind, let's examine the given expression.

- Option I might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that ${x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)$ can't be written as 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),
$$

where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because it lacks the particular solution term ${x}_{p}(t).$

- Option II might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that $5\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$ can't be written as 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),
$$

where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier $5$ next to the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$

- Option III might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that $-3\cdot {x}_{2}(t)-{x}_{p}(t)$ can't be written as 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),
$$

where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier $-1$ next to the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None".

Additonally, the linearity principle for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if x1(t), x2(t),…,xk(t) are solutions to a homogeneous linear system x′(t)=Ax(t), then any linear combination c1x1(t)+c2x2(t)+⋯+ckxk(t) with c1,c2,…,ck∈R is also a solution of the same homogeneous system.

With that in mind, let's examine the given expression.

  • Option I might be not a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that x1(t)−x2(t) can't be written as xh(t)+xp(t), where xh(t) is a solution of the homogeneous system, because it lacks the particular solution term xp(t).

  • Option II might be not a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that 5⋅xp(t) can't be written as xh(t)+xp(t), where xh(t) is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier 5 next to the particular solution xp(t).

  • Option III might be not a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that −3⋅x2(t)−xp(t) can't be written as xh(t)+xp(t), where xh(t) is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier −1 next to the particular solution xp(t).

Therefore, the correct answer is "None".
